issues.item: Triggers: Female Presence: Being alone with women
issues.explanation: For a childhood trauma of witnessing domestic violence, the trigger pattern is strongly male-linked ('being alone with men') but also includes 'being alone with women' without any corresponding formulation or symptom content explaining why both genders would be equivalently triggering. That broadens the trigger profile in a way that is hard to connect to the rest of the report, which is centered on interpersonal threat from others who might harm him rather than gender-nonspecific social presence.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Driving: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Driving/being a passenger in a vehicle' is difficult to link to the reported trauma and the rest of the profile. No other trigger, threat, or memory item involves transport, accidents, escape, or vehicles, so this strategy appears to address a symptom domain not represented elsewhere in the five components.

vignette:
Rangi Tuilagi is an eighteen-year-old Samoan-American male who presents for his initial intake following a referral from his university's student health service. He works part-time as a junior project manager at a small construction consultancy, a role that places him regularly in the company of older men on job sites and in site offices. He is currently in a romantic relationship, though he reports that his partner has grown increasingly concerned about changes in his behaviour over recent months. His PCL-5 score of 55 places him firmly within the severe range of post-traumatic stress symptomatology.

Rangi grew up in a household in which his father's drinking was a fixed and threatening constant. What he describes, haltingly and in fragments across the first two sessions, is less a single event than a sustained landscape of fear - though one night in particular appears to anchor much of what he now carries. He was around seven years old. He remembers the smell first: the sharp, sweet-sour odour of alcohol that would drift under his bedroom door and tell him, before he heard anything, what kind of night it was going to be. Then the sound of his father's bicycle being dropped against the front steps. Then his mother's voice, low and placating, and then the impact of something - he cannot say what - and her cry. He recalls pressing himself into the corner behind his bed, watching the strip of light under the door. The rest, he says, is missing. He does not know how the night ended. He does not know how he got to school the next morning. What remains are those pieces - the smell, the sound of the bicycle, the light under the door - vivid and unordered, surfacing without warning and carrying with them the same paralysing terror he felt as a small boy in the dark.

In the years since, Rangi finished high school with strong grades and moved into work earlier than most of his peers. On the surface he appeared capable and self-possessed. But the fragments never organised themselves into a coherent past. Remembering does not feel like remembering - it feels, he says, like being dropped back into that hallway, heart hammering, certain that something terrible is still about to happen.

At the consultancy, his days require him to attend morning briefings in small site offices with male colleagues and subcontractors. He has come to watch the men around him with a careful, exhausting vigilance - noting who raises their voice, who stands too close, who smells of last night's drinking. When a senior colleague arrived at a Tuesday briefing with alcohol on his breath, Rangi left the room on a fabricated errand and did not return. His manager has noted his absences. Riding his bicycle to the office, which he does most mornings, has become a source of dread he cannot fully explain to himself - there is something about the particular sound of tyres on gravel, or the act of leaning the frame against a wall, that causes his chest to tighten before he has even reached the door. He has begun locking his apartment compulsively each evening, checking the door handle four or five times before he can sit down, and again before he sleeps. Ordinary sounds - a door slamming in the corridor, a raised voice from a neighbouring flat - cause him to startle badly enough that his partner has started warning him before she enters a room.

To manage the edges of all this, Rangi smokes heavily and drinks most evenings, aware of the irony and troubled by it. He has also begun avoiding social gatherings, withdrawing from a friendship group he valued through his final year of school. His partner, who does not yet know the full shape of what happened in his childhood, has told him she feels shut out.

What finally brought him to the student health service was a performance review in which his manager raised concerns about reliability. Rangi had worked hard for this role and had come to believe that his competence was the one thing that could not be taken from him. The possibility that the past might cost him that too was, he said quietly, more than he could sit with alone. What he hopes for, most of all, is to understand why the pieces will not fit together - and whether they ever could.
